title: How would you reshard this database as it grows, without downtime?
summary: Resharding live is a mechanics question, not a hand-wave. Learn the dual-write, backfill, cutover sequence that lets you rebalance data without ever taking writes offline.

slides.markdown:
"Add more shards" is the easy half of the answer and the half that undersells the real difficulty: moving live data between shard layouts without a maintenance window. The interviewer wants the actual mechanics — how do writes stay correct while data is mid-move?

The standard pattern is dual-write, backfill, verify, cutover, cleanup. Each step exists to answer one question: what happens to a write that lands *during* the migration? This topic walks that sequence concretely.

Ask: **is this a planned rebalance, or a reaction to an already-hot shard?** A planned rebalance gives you time to run the migration slowly and verify carefully. A reactive resharding — a shard already struggling under load — means the migration itself has to be careful not to add more load to the very shard that's already overwhelmed.

Also worth asking: how large is the dataset, and what's an acceptable dual-write window — hours, or days? These answers shape how aggressively you can run the backfill.

Structure it as: **dual-write to old and new layout, backfill historical data in the background, verify, cut reads over, then stop dual-writing.** Every new write during the migration goes to both the old and new shard layout, so nothing is lost regardless of when cutover happens.

Meanwhile a background job copies existing rows from old to new layout. Only once the backfill catches up to "live" and the two layouts agree do you flip reads to the new layout — and only after that do you retire the old one.

![Five-stage resharding timeline: dual-write, backfill, verify, cutover, cleanup](assets/resharding-stages.svg)

The key detail this diagram carries: dual-writing starts at the very beginning and doesn't stop until after cutover is verified — it's the safety net across the entire migration, not just the first step.

Each stage has a clear exit condition before moving to the next: backfill exits when it catches up to live writes; verify exits when checksums match; cutover exits once reads are confirmed correct on the new layout.

assets.alt: Five-stage resharding timeline: dual-write, backfill, verify, cutover, cleanup

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: flipping reads only after backfill lag hits zero
slides.markdown:
The exact trigger for cutover matters: don't flip reads to the new layout until the backfill's **lag** — the gap between the newest row it has copied and the newest row in the live system — reaches zero. Flip too early and reads against the new layout return stale or missing data.

In practice this means monitoring a lag metric (rows behind, or seconds behind) throughout the backfill, and only proceeding once it's sustained at zero for a safety window, not just touched zero once and bounced back up under load.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: keeping the dual-write window short
slides.markdown:
Dual-writing doubles write cost for the entire migration duration, so the practical goal is to keep that window as short as safely possible. The lever is **throttling the backfill against production traffic** — running it aggressively during off-peak hours and backing off during peak load, rather than a flat constant rate that either starves the backfill or competes with live traffic.

A backfill that respects production load takes longer in wall-clock time but avoids becoming the incident it was meant to prevent.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
Say this explicitly: **dual-writing avoids downtime, but it doubles write cost and adds real complexity for the whole migration window — and that window is usually longer than people expect.** It's not a quick trick; it's a sustained operational cost.

Every write path in the application needs to know about both layouts during this time, every bug in either write path now risks divergence between old and new data, and the team needs monitoring for lag and divergence the whole time. Naming this cost, not just the technique, is what a senior answer sounds like.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: how do you verify the new layout before cutover?
slides.markdown:
Name concrete checks, not "we test it." Row counts per shard, checksums or hashes over row ranges compared between old and new layouts, and spot-checking a sample of individual records field-by-field. Automate this comparison to run continuously during backfill, not as a single check right before cutover.

For an especially sensitive dataset, consider a **shadow read** period: serve reads from the old layout as the source of truth while also querying the new layout and comparing results silently, surfacing any mismatch before it ever reaches a real user.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: the cutover reveals a data mismatch
slides.markdown:
This is exactly why cutover isn't the point of no return in a well-designed migration — you should be able to flip reads back to the old layout immediately, since dual-writing means it's still current. Roll back first, then investigate.

Once rolled back, fix forward: find the specific divergence (a race condition in the dual-write path, an edge case the backfill missed), patch it, re-run verification, and only attempt cutover again once the mismatch is resolved and re-verified. Don't force a cutover through a known mismatch under schedule pressure.

**Wrong belief:** "We'll schedule a maintenance window, take writes offline, migrate everything, then bring it back up."

**Why it's wrong:** at any real scale, the dataset is too large to move within an acceptable downtime window, and modern products rarely have an acceptable downtime window at all. It also removes your safety net — if something goes wrong mid-migration, there's no old layout still receiving live writes to fall back to.

**Correct model:** dual-write and backfill live, keeping the old layout fully current throughout, so cutover is a reversible flip rather than a one-way door.

"I'd dual-write every new record to both the old and new shard layouts, then run a throttled background job to backfill historical data into the new layout. I'd only cut reads over once backfill lag sustains at zero and checksums between layouts match — and I'd keep dual-writing until after cutover is verified, so I can roll back instantly if a mismatch shows up. Only once the new layout has proven correct under live traffic would I retire the old one."
